neighbours.label: ' over' right after roll/rolled/rolling (the phrasal verb 'roll over'), literal (flipping over) or figurative (steamrolling a team)
fire: When the vet scratched his belly, the old retriever happily rolled over and stuck all four paws in the air.
The champions were rolling over every opponent in the league, winning by double digits week after week.
A delivery truck carrying crates of oranges rolled over on the highway, blocking both lanes for hours.
At the yoga class we practiced rolling over from our backs onto our stomachs without using our hands.
The senator refused to roll over and accept the new budget, vowing to fight it in committee.
During the storm, our small boat nearly rolled over when a huge wave struck it from the side.
Toddlers usually learn to roll over by themselves somewhere around the fourth or fifth month of life.
Critics said the board simply rolled over for the investors instead of defending the founder's vision.
quiet: Our retriever wagged his tail and stuck all four paws in the air as the vet came near.
Every opponent in the league was crushed by the visiting champions, who won by double digits week after week.
Crates of oranges spilled across the highway after a delivery truck stalled, blocking both lanes for hours.
Our yoga teacher had us stretch both arms over our heads while breathing slowly and evenly.
Looking over the new budget carefully, the senator vowed to fight it in committee next week.
Waves crashed against the side as our small boat drifted over the shallow reef during the storm.
Most babies learn to crawl by themselves somewhere around the eighth or ninth month of life.
